answers.answer: Replication copies data changes between servers; a replica is each maintained copy. It keeps copies of the same data, while sharding partitions data into different groups; each group can itself have replicas. Copies can serve additional reads, be near users, and take over after a server fails. Uninterrupted service still requires read routing and safe takeover, freshness requires catching up, and adding read replicas does not automatically add write capacity. A new replica starts from a snapshot, a copy at a known point, and follows a change log recording later source changes. Applying a change updates replica data so queries can see it. The snapshot and starting log position must agree to avoid missing or incorrectly applying changes; required source order must be preserved so an older dependent change does not undo a newer value. Replicas track progress to resume after disconnects. Receiving records is separate from applying them, so received data can remain invisible to reads.

evidence.quote: Copies data changes between servers. Each maintained copy is a replica.
Read routing and a safe takeover process are separate design work; a second copy does not configure either automatically.
Adding read replicas can increase read capacity. It does not automatically increase the number of writes the system can handle.
The initial copy and starting log position must agree. Otherwise the handoff can miss changes or apply them incorrectly.
The replica tracks its progress so it can resume after a disconnect. Receiving a change and applying it are separate steps.
The replica updated its data so queries can see the change.

answers.answer: Asynchronous replication lets the writing server acknowledge success before a replica confirms the change. Acknowledgement says the configured success condition was met; it does not prove another server has the write. For example, the primary accepts and acknowledges a write, then fails permanently before sending it. Promoting a replica that never received it loses that confirmed write. The latency benefit is avoiding the replica wait, at the cost of possibly older reads and recent-write loss. Synchronous replication waits for confirmation from required replicas before success. Specify which replicas or how many must confirm and the stage: received may mean only memory, durable storage survives a restart, and applied means queries can see it. Waiting for durable copies protects against losing the writer but adds delay and dependency on replicas; if an unavailable replica leaves too few required confirmations, writes can stall. Asynchronous acknowledgement need not wait for that replica. Synchronous success need not involve all replicas, and durable or received confirmation alone does not establish that even the confirming replica has applied the change. It protects only against specified failures, not loss of every copy or accidental logical changes.

evidence.quote: The writing server can acknowledge success before a replica confirms the change. Acknowledgement means the configured success condition was met, not that every copy has the data.
If the writing server fails permanently before sending a confirmed change, a replacement replica will not have that change.
The replica has the change, possibly only in memory.
The replica saved it to storage that can survive a restart.
Waiting for durable copies protects against losing the writing server. It adds delay, and writes can stall if too few required replicas respond.
Choose the required replica set or count and acknowledgement stage. This protects against specified failures, not loss of every copy or accidental logical changes.

answers.answer: Replication lag means a replica is behind the source in receiving or applying changes. A successful write can be followed by an older replica read because that replica has not applied the write yet, even if it has received it. Read-after-write here means later reads include your own completed change or newer state. Reading from the still-authoritative primary holding the write avoids waiting for replica application but concentrates load and requires knowing the correct authority after failover. Alternatively, wait for evidence that the selected replica applied that specific write; this adds delay and can fail. A fixed sleep or low average lag does not establish visibility of that write. Accepting stale reads permits delay-tolerant reads to use replicas without a freshness wait, distributing read load, but accepts older results. Neither routing nor waiting can recover a write already lost during failover. A leader is a server that accepts writes for data and whose changes are copied. A single leader provides one place to order writes, with followers copying and a failover process needed to replace it. Multiple leaders accept writes on several servers and exchange changes, allowing nearby writes but requiring a conflict rule when they independently edit the same item; latest-timestamp selection may discard a valid edit. In a leaderless arrangement, any coordinating server can send requests to the replicas holding the data, wait for a configured reply count, and repair differences; concurrent versions still need reconciliation. More write-accepting servers do not automatically remove conflicts or guarantee one current value, and these topology names alone do not specify synchronous versus asynchronous replication.

evidence.quote: A replica is behind the source in receiving or applying changes. State which stage a lag measurement describes; data received but not applied is not yet visible to reads.
Later reads include your own completed change or newer state. Read from the authoritative primary holding the write, or wait for evidence that the selected replica applied that specific change.
Primary reads concentrate load and require correct authority after failover. Waiting for a replica adds delay and can fail. Routing alone cannot recover a write already lost during failover.
One server accepts writes for a set of data. Followers copy its changes.
If two leaders change the same item independently, the system needs a conflict rule. Choosing the latest timestamp can discard another valid edit.
Concurrent versions still need reconciliation; no topology name guarantees one current value or conflict-free updates.

answers.answer: Failover moves a failed server's responsibilities to another server. In a single-leader system, promotion means making the selected suitable replica the leader, and applications must be redirected to it. The replacement must be sufficiently current for the required write-loss target: its progress affects which recent writes survive. Silence alone does not prove the old leader is dead; its network may be broken while it still accepts writes. Fencing prevents it from continuing to write, for example by shutting it down or blocking access. This avoids split brain, in which two servers both act as sole leader and accept conflicting changes. Acknowledged asynchronous writes absent from the replacement can be lost. A healthy replica may already have copied an accidental deletion, so current copies cannot necessarily recover the previous state. A backup preserves an earlier recoverable state, and point-in-time recovery restores it and replays retained logs up to a chosen time, such as just before deletion. Retention and available logs limit recoverable history. A restore test must reconstruct usable application data and measure recovery duration; mere file existence proves neither. An untested backup or a current replica alone does not establish recoverable history or recovery time. The lesson does not specify a particular replica eligibility algorithm; suitability must be assessed against the chosen recovery requirements.

evidence.quote: Moves a failed server's responsibilities to another server. In a single-leader system, the process selects a suitable replica, promotes it to leader, and redirects application connections. How current that replica is affects whether recent writes survive.
A missing response does not prove the old leader stopped. Its network connection can be broken while it still accepts writes.
Happens when two servers both act as the sole leader. They can accept conflicting changes.
Prevents the old leader from continuing to write, for example by shutting it down or blocking its access.
Replication also copies unwanted changes. If someone deletes the wrong records, replicas can apply that deletion too.
Retention and available logs bound recoverable history. Restore tests must reconstruct usable application data and measure how long recovery takes; file existence alone proves neither.

answers.answer: First learn the maximum acceptable loss of acknowledged writes and the failures that must be survived, how stale reporting reads may be, whether any reads require seeing their own writes, acceptable write delay or failure while waiting for copies, allowable downtime, and how far back historical recovery must reach. A policy supported by the lesson is single-leader writes with synchronous durable confirmation from a selected replica set or count chosen for those failure and loss requirements. Durable confirmation reduces the risk of losing acknowledged writes if the writer fails, but adds commit delay and can stall writes when too few required replicas respond. The supplied requirements do not determine an exact count, latency budget, loss limit, or downtime target. Route delay-tolerant reporting reads to replicas within the accepted freshness requirements; use the authoritative primary or proof that a selected replica applied the specific write for freshness-sensitive reads. Durable acknowledgement alone does not make every replica read current. Prepare failover that chooses a suitable sufficiently current replica, fences the old leader, promotes the replacement, and redirects clients. Keep backups and retained change logs for earlier-state recovery because replication also copies accidental deletions. Monitor replication progress, receiving/application lag, health, and write waits; exercise failover and historical restore, checking write survival, usable restored application data, and measured recovery time against targets. Account for storage, network, and operating work. Replication alone promises neither zero loss nor uninterrupted writes: guarantees depend on acknowledgement stages and required copies, failures can destroy all copies, logical mistakes propagate, and network splits force operations needing unreachable agreement to wait or fail. Independent operation instead requires handling old reads and conflicts.

evidence.quote: Choose acceptable acknowledged-write loss, read freshness, write latency and recovery time before choosing replica settings.

Delay-tolerant reads can use replicas. Freshness-sensitive reads need suitable routing or progress checks. Waiting for durable replica acknowledgements narrows some loss windows but adds commit delay and dependence on those replicas.
Copies consume storage, network and operating work. Monitor replication progress, lag, health and write waits; exercise failover and historical restore against the required recovery targets.
During a network split, operations that need agreement with unreachable copies must wait or fail. Independent operation instead needs explicit handling of old reads and conflicting writes.
Replication helps keep service running after a server failure. Backups and retained logs help recover earlier data.
Choose the required replica set or count and acknowledgement stage. This protects against specified failures, not loss of every copy or accidental logical changes.
